This paleomagnetic study of =700 specimens yielded a normal segment in all 5 profiles and an excursive segment in 3 pro- files. The normal zones give, in most cases, significantly different directions which sug- gests that they are not strictly coeval and that deposition rates in this till are highly variable from one point to the next. Overall, they give a virtual geomagnetic pole located at 273.1øW, 73.0øN (p = 1.7 , am = 2.6). Simi- larly the 3 excursive zones are not exactly coeval. Assuming the remanence reflects a single excursion then the pole appears to swing from mid-Africa to mid-South Pacific, and then back to the normal Arctic pole. This polar sequence and the apparent paleofield intensi- ties are notably similar to those found in aboriginal fireplaces at Lake Mungo, Australia. The Meadowcliffe Till is the first Ontario till to yield evidence of recording a geomag- netic field excursion(s). Accordingly its pa- leomagnetic age is set at 30,500 + 1,500 yr B.P. which is within the 8,000 yr window per- mitted by the single radiocarbon dates from below and above the till. The small difference in longitude between the poles from the two sections is not statistically significant, but could be due either to apparent polar wander or relative motion between the two sections. The small difference in longitude between the poles from the two sections is not statistically significant, but could be due either to apparent polar wander or relative motion between the two sections. Also, fluid inclusion studies have shown repeatedly that the Mississippi Valley-type ores were probably deposited from low-temperature, high-sa- linity brines (Roedder, 1967, 1977a and b). The Vi- burnum mines, regionally and locally, are structurally high and on the flanks of a major sedimentary basin in a cratonic setting. The ore is stratabound, confined to the Upper Cainbrian Bonneterre Dolostone, and of simple mineralogy, consisting predominantly of galena, sphalerite, marcasite, and pyrite. The mines are largely associated with drapes over highs of the hummocky Precambrian basement or within strati- graphic traps adjacent to monoclinal dips to the west- erly trending basin. The lead isotopes are complex and have been regarded as derived from sedimentary sources (Doe and Delevaux, 1972, Sverjensky et al., 1979). Sulfur isotopes show a wide spread and are likewise considered to be derived from sedimentary sources, probably from sulfate deposited within more restricted facies of the Bonneterre host rock. The metamorphism of these rocks took place under conditions of granulite facies but, according to Paavola (1976), the pressure was not very high during the recrystallization. Plutonic gabbros and diori- tes from this area contain large amounts of magnetite, thus making it possible to conduct paleomagnetic investigations. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

matitic paragneisses of diverse compositions. These gneisses are quartz dioritic or dioritic in com- position with mica- and hornblende gneiss and amphibolite horizons. Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. These basement rocks in the Jonsa area are cut by diabase dykes (Fig. 3) running approxi- mately in an E-W or SE-NW direction. Paleomagnetic data on the Main Sulphide Ore Belt in Finland are coherent but differ clearly from those obtained on the Archean basement area immediately north of it. The coherent magnetization in ithe Belt could have been caused by (i) axial uplift, (ii) a plate suture along the Belt or (iii) a short-time igneous pulse. The last interpretation is accepted since it agrees with the radiometric age data. Thus the paleomagnetic measurements in the area date the same thermal events as do the radiometric U-Pb age determinations, and the shape of the APW curve is thereby verified. A paleomagnetic pole determined for dykes intersecting the Archean basement block lies off the accepted APW curve which possibly need to be corrected. The magmatic pulse between 1880— 1840 Ma may have been associated with a plate collision or with a deep fluid convection producing the sulphide ore precipitation within the Belt. K. J. Paleomagnetic data on the Main Sulphide Ore Belt in Finland are coherent but differ clearly from those obtained on the Archean basement area immediately north of it. The coherent magnetization in ithe Belt could have been caused by (i) axial uplift, (ii) a plate suture along the Belt or (iii) a short-time igneous pulse. The last interpretation is accepted since it agrees with the radiometric age data. Thus the paleomagnetic measurements in the area date the same thermal events as do the radiometric U-Pb age determinations, and the shape of the APW curve is thereby verified. A paleomagnetic pole determined for dykes intersecting the Archean basement block lies off the accepted APW curve which possibly need to be corrected. The magmatic pulse between 1880— 1840 Ma may have been associated with a plate collision or with a deep fluid convection producing the sulphide ore precipitation within the Belt. K. J. The directions of remanent magnetization measured inside the belt vary very little (Fig. 1). This coherency is well seen in the cluster formed by the paleomagnetic poles of the rocks in

between the Belt and the Archean craton area since Svecokarelian time. The simplest tectonic model to explain the observed paleomagnetic character of the areas now studied is axial uplift or subsiding of the Belt in relation to the basement com- plex in the northeast. The homogeneous and coherent remanence measured on the erosion surface in the Belt area could have been created in the rocks of the rising Belt in a manner similar to that described by Beckman et al. (1977) and Morgan (1976) from Green- land (see also Ueno and Irving 1976). The coherent magnetization would have taken place when the rock units passed the blocking or Curie-temperature in the crust (zero-line of Neuvonen 1961). If however, this type of uplift magnetiza- tion takes place in rock units that are of simi- lar age but belonging to two adjacent blocks with a different rate of uplift, the rocks should show different magnetic directions on the erosion surface. Closer to the Bothnian Sea, at the north- western end of the Belt metamorphism has taken place mainly under conditions of am- phibolite facies. Plutonic gabbros and diori- tes from this area contain large amounts of magnetite, thus making it possible to conduct paleomagnetic investigations. The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area North of Kuopio, the boundary between the Svecokarelian rocks and the Archean basement runs subparallel to the Belt (Fig. 1). The Nilsiä—Varpaisjärvi area lies about 50 km north of Kuopio and the majority of the rocks in this area belong to the Archean basement complex. It is divided into two parts by the N-S-trending Proterozoic (Sveco- karelian) Tahkomäki quartzite ridge (Fig. 3). On the eastern side of the quartzite ridge, in the Lake Syväri area, the basement com- prises mainly of banded and migmatitic paragneisses of diverse compo

matitic paragneisses of diverse compositions. These gneisses are quartz dioritic or dioritic in com- position with mica- and hornblende gneiss and amphibolite horizons. Narrow cordierite- gneiss bands also occur. This paragneiss com- plex is weakly magnetized and was not studied paleomagnetically. On the northwestern side of the Tahkomäki quartzite ridge, in the Jonsa area, northeast of Varpaisjärvi (Fig. 3), the basement differs from other Archean granite gneiss types of Finland particularly in its orthopyroxene content. The rock here is highly metamor- phosed and forms a clearly limited, separate block of basement. It has a high magnetite content and is seen as a strong magnetic anomaly on the aeromagnetic map. The remanent magnetization of the rocks of the complex being very high, it is suitable for paleomagnetic investigations. These basement rocks in the Jonsa area are cut by diabase dykes (Fig. 3) running approxi- mately in an E-W or SE-NW direction. The width of the dykes varies from a few centi- metres to about 150 metres. The contacts be- tween the diabase and the wall rock are always very sharp, and chilled margins are usual. The diabase dyke rock is very homo- geneous, massive and fine- or medium-grain- ed. Ophitic texture is common. The best pre- served dy

A second set of intersecting dykes occurs in the Nilsiä area (Fig. 3). These dykes are fine- grained, massive and homogeneous. The con- tacts with the wall rock are sharp and apophyses are common. The dykes are from a few centimetres to 4—5 metres wide. Their direction varies between N15°W and N85°W (345°—275°). The dip is subvertical. The mineral composition of these dykes includes plagioclase, quartz, biotite and horn- blende with accessory epidote, sphene, apatite and magnetite. Plagioclase occurs locally as intensely zoned (An 35.25) laths, 1.5—2 mm in size. According to the classification of Streckeisen (1976), these dykes have a tonali- tic or quartz dioritic composition. They can be correlated with the tonalitic dykes de- scribed by Huhma (1975 and 1981) from North Karelia, with an age between 1860 and 1830 Ma. These dykes have a weak but rather hard remanent magnetization. The lithology and paleo- magnetic data obtained will be described and discussed below. Additional paleomagnetic results already available from the north- western end of the Belt and from the Iisalmi area (see Fig. 1) will be included in the Dis- cussion. Radiometric age data and lead iso- tope values will also be considered in drawing conclusions about the origin and evolution of the Belt. The lithology of the area Lithologically, the Belt is not well defined and its borders cannot be drawn exactly. It consists of series of metasediments and meta- volcanics deformed, recrystallized and folded during the Svecokarelian (1800—1900 Ma) orogeny. These schists and gneisses are pene- trated by various of intrusive rocks mainly of synkinematic character. An area typical of the Belt is met with in the southeastern part of the zone in the Haukivesi area (Figs. 1 and 2). The Jotnian sequence is extensively cut by (‘post-Jotnian’) dolerites mostly in the form of sills and thick SE-NW dykes; these are fresh ophitic dolerites comprising labradorite feldspar, augite, olivine, ilmenite and magnetite. Real progress in under- standing the Precambrian geomagnetic field is hampered by the paucity of suitable volcanic andlor sedimentary suites. Studies to date on the ca. 1100 Ma Keweenawan lavas of North America (eg. A. PIPER and ROBERT L. ShlITH Piper, J. D. A. & Smith, R. L., 1980 10 15: Palaeomagnetism of the Jotnian lavas and sediments and post-Jotnian dolerites of central Scandinavia. Geologiska Foreningens i Stockholm Forhandlingar, Vol. 102, Pt. 2, pp. 67-81. Stockholm. ISSN 0016-786X. Alternating field and thermal demagnetisation studies of lavas and sediments assigned to the Proterozoic Jotnian of western Sweden (Dalarna) and eastern Norway are reported. Hematite is the predominant remanence carrier in the sediments. These locally record a dipolar axis of magnetisation D= 14" and I = 10". but the bulk of the sediments, including the western part of the outcrop and all of the upper sequence, have a characteristic remanence ca. D= 160", 1=35". interpreted as a magnetic overprint during the Sveconorwegian mobile episode (1 100-800 hla). The lavas have low deuteric oxidation states but were subjected to widespread hematisation during later hydrothermal activity.

The thermal demagnetization tests on the dolerites indicated a discrete blocking temperature inter- val of 550400°C. Considerations of the effects of slow cooling and thermal remanent magnetization (TRM) have been made by Pul- laiah et al. (1975), who showed that, theorFtica1- ly, the remanence in magnetite with blocking temperatures within 50°C of the Curie point can survive lower amphibolite facies metamorphism. Generally the dif- ferences between the different methods were less than 2” and no systematic error was observed. The sampling sites are shown on the map(Fig. 1). For the measurements, one to four cylindrical specimens, 2.4 cm in height and 2.5 cm in diame- ter were obtained from each sample. The NRM was measured on a 85 Hz UGF-JR 3 or a 7 Hz Digico spinner magnetometer. Alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization techniques were used to remove unstable soft magnetization and to isolate the characteristic stable magnetic component. In both methods the demagnetiza- tion was done in fields of less than 10 nT. Pilot specimens from each site were step-wise de- magnetized to peak fields of 100 mT. Generally stable end-points for the magnetic vectors were obtained in the range 3040 mT, an exception being site SF for which a field of 80 mT was necessary to reach stability. After the pilot test the remaining specimens were demagnetized in five steps to 50 mT, and for site SF in eight steps to 100 mT. Thermal demagnetization was done in 13-14 steps to 600450°C on specimens from each site. All five samples from a site close to the western peak on mount Ottfjallet proved unsta- ble during progressive demagnetization and the results from this site were rejected. The dolerites of the main part of the Sarv Nappe contain, after progressive alternating field and thermal demagnetization, a stable magnetic component of decl. 21.4". incl. -9.1". ass= 12.4'. k= 11.3. This gives a geomagnetic pole at lat. 21"N, long. 170"E which is in agreement with published Silurian-Devonian poles from Fennoscandia. This together with a simple 'fold test' implies that the Proterozoic dolerites became remagnetized during the Caledonian orogeny. The magnetic directions from the dolerites in the northern part of the nappe, the Ottfjallet block, indicate that this area has rotated ca. 100-1 10" counterclockwise in relation to the rest of the nappe. 0 Palaeomagnetism. pole positions, remagnetization, rotation, dykes, tholeiitic dolerite. Palaeomagnetism has had its main success in establishing the presence of large-scale move- ments in the Earth's crust but the method is also applicable in many other fields such as the study of events in a period of orogeny. For example, the measurements of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), can give information about the magnetization build-up in relation to the metamorphic history of different units, in- cluding studies of relative movements. The Geotraverse, from Ostersund in Sweden across the Scandinavian Caledonides to Trondheim in Norway (Annersten 1973; Bylund et al. 1976) presents numerous possibilities for studies of this kind, and an obvious subject for such work is the well preserved parts of the Sarv Nappe with its conspicuous swarm of tholeiitic dolerite dykes. Conclusions The results of this study imply that the original NRM of the Scanian hyperite dolerites and sye- nites was overprinted or obliterated due to events related to the Svecononvegian orogeny, viz. regional heating, uplift, and slow cooling. This later remanence became directed along the ambient geomagnetic field. Later events in the Protogine Zone and the intersecting Tornquist Lineament, e.g. the intrusion of a large swarm of dolerite dykes, did not affect this NRM. The palaeornagnetic data for the whole Sveco- norwegian belt, including the Protogine Zone, show a complicated pattern due to differences in thermal influence, magnetic minerals with varying blocking-temperature spectra, and diffe- rent rates of cooling and uplift in the Sveco- norwegian belt and the Protogine Zone. Two important tectonic lineaments intersect in Scania (SkAne), southernmost Sweden. One is the zone separating the Precambrian Fennoscan- dian Shield from central Europe and its sedimentary cover and the other is the Protogine Zone (PZ) which constitutes the border between the entirely different Proterozoic terrains of the southwestern and central Fennoscandian Shield. Movements and intrusions in these zones have contributed to the mosaic pattern and the mix of Proterozoic gneisses, granites and Phanerozoic sediments that form the geology of Scania. The purpose of this paper is to present a study of the magnetic properties of intrusive hyperite doler- ites and syenites from the Scanian part of the PZ in relation to their situation in the intersection between those tectonic lineaments. The Protogine Zone - other names sometimes used for this feature are the Schistosity Zone, The Gothide Front, the Svecononvegian Front - trends from Scania northwards across southern Sweden to Nonvay where it is cut by the Scan- dinavian Caledonides (Fig. 1). It separates the Svecononvegian southwestern corner of the Fennsocandian Shield from its central Sveco- karelian part. There is at present a running discussion whether the PZ is part of a global suture, the scar of a plate collision between a "Grenvillian-Svecononvegian" plate 'and the Laurentian-Fennoscandian plate or whether it is an intrashield structure along which movements have occurred intermittently during the Precam- brian, i.e. Donaldson et al. INTRODUCTION The occurrence of glaciation towards the end of Precambrian times has been widely recognised in all continents, except Antarctica (Harland, 1964; Harland and Rudwick, 1964; Dunn et al., 1971; Crawford and Daily, 1971; Williams, 1974, 1975; and others). At least three distinct glacial episodes are recorded in several continents, particularly in Africa and Australia (Wil- liams, 1975) the oldest is the Gnesjo glaciation some 960 million years ago, the Startian was some 770 million years ago, and the youngest, the Varangian, occurred some 615 million years ago. The duration of each of these episodes is even less certain than their age, but it is generally thought that the thickness of theglacial sequences indicate episodes of tens of millions of years duration. (2) A "normal" high-latitude glaciation at a time of rapid polar motion so that the glacial debris are not, in fact, synchronous, but somewhat different in age in different areas (Crawford and Daily, 1971; Piper, 1973; McElhinny et al., 1974). (3) Climatic oddities arising because the Earth's axis of rotation lay close to the ecliptic so that there was, effectively, six months day and six months night, the effect of which would oscillate from excessive cold to excessive heat depending on "normal" precessions of the Earth's rotational axis (Williams, 1974, 1975). Clearly, the main test between such models is that of the degree of synchroneity between the different deposits, but such speculations can be reduced if it could be demonstrated that all the glaciations did, in fact, occur at high latitudes as this would, in itself, mean that the glaciations could not be coeval. Palaeoclimatic indicators of palaeo- latitude are notoriously ambiguous, although the presence of thick carbonate sequences, with evidence of evaporites and the presence of stellate structures within some Eocambrian glaciation sequences, such as in northwestern Scotland, would imply low latitudes. Attempts have been made to evaluate the probable palaeolatitudes of several Late Precam- brian glacial sequences by interpolation for this time within the existing polar wander paths, but such estimates suffer from the imprecision in the dating of both the polar wander curves themselves and of the glacial depos- its. Palaeomagnetic observations directly on these glacial deposits, or in- timately associated beds, are sparse although observations in Greenland 327 and Norway (Harland and Bidgood, 1959; Bidgood and Harland, 1961), North America (Morris, 1977), Africa and Australia (McWilliams, 1977; McWilliams and McElhinny, 1980) and Greenland and Scotland (Tarling, 1974) all seem to indicate low latitudes, although some of the Australia palaeolatitudes are as high as 60 ° (McWilliams, 1977). In order to extend the evidence for the low latitude origin of the Eocambrian glacial deposits in northwestern Scotland, a more extensive collection of samples has been made in three localities which deliberately included intimately associated thick sequences of limestones and dolostones which immediately preceded the deposition of the glacial tillites and mixtites. Since the beds suffered low-grade metamorphism during the Caledonian orogeny (Spencer, 1971; Borradaile and Johnson, 1973), there were also the possibilities of re-magnetization and distortion of the magnetic minerals during the formation of the cleavage. Abouzakhm and Tarling (1975), working on the same sample collection, showed that the dynamic metamorphism did not apparently affect the palaeomagnetic directions of the rocks studied as the palaeomagnetic directions were unrelated to the petrofabric of the magnetites. 328 Re-examining the results given by Abouzakhm (1974) and Abouzakhm and Tarling (1975) shows that although the remanent direction and the mag- netic susceptibility dependent orientations are unrelated, the magnetic fabric is not a primary depositional fabric, but is of strain-controlled origin. The maximum susceptibility (k,) lies normal to the bedding plane and the mini- mum susceptibility (k3) was close to the intersection of the bedding and cleavage planes (fig.2 in Abouzakhm and Tarling, 1975). Samples from two regions and from a range of rock types in northwest Scotland have remanences that are stable to thermal and alternating magnetic field demagnetisation. Normal and reversed directions for different areas are also in closer agreement after correc- tion for the different tectonic tilt in the different areas. These data are therefore thought to substantiate previous evidence proposed for the low latitude of deposition of the Eocambrian tillites and associated thick limestones and dolomites. Samples from two regions and from a range of rock types in northwest Scotland have remanences that are stable to thermal and alternating magnetic field demagnetisation. Normal and reversed directions for different areas are also in closer agreement after correc- tion for the different tectonic tilt in the different areas. The age of the remanence is pre- Devonian and most considerations indicate, but do not prove, an Eocambrian age. These data are therefore thought to substantiate previous evidence proposed for the low latitude of deposition of the Eocambrian tillites and associated thick limestones and dolomites. On this basis, it is not thought that the climatic changes indicated by the nature of the sediments can be attributed to rapid polar wandering during this period. The data do, however, indicate that the glaciation not only took place at sea level, but at latitudes which indicate that these glaciations at this time could represent a world-wide glacial event. Mountain glaciations can, of course, occur at many times throughout the history of the Earth, but extensive ice sheets are rare. The formation of younger ice sheets, such as the Sakmarian (basal Permian) glaciation of the Gondwanan continents and the Quaternary ice sheet glaciation can be understood, in very general terms, in the context of specific palaeogeographic conditions existing at high latitudes (Tarling, 1978), but these Eocambrian glaciations are particularly intriguing as they appear to be world-wide in extent and do not appear to be associated with orogenic events (and hence are not mountain glaciations) and the interglacial deposits frequently suggest that they were formed in very low latitudes. In order to extend the evidence for the low latitude origin of the Eocambrian glacial deposits in northwestern Scotland, a more extensive collection of samples has been made in three localities which deliberately included intimately associated thick sequences of limestones and dolostones which immediately preceded the deposition of the glacial tillites and mixtites.
